fetched_contents.text: Are Speech Delays Genetic? ‍ Prospective parents undergoing IVF and preimplantation genetic testing (PGT) – such as those using Orchid’s whole-genome embryo screening – often ask, “Are speech delays genetic?” This concern is understandable: speech and language development is a complex process influenced by both genes and environment. Below we provide a clear overview of what speech delays are, the genetic contributions to speech and language development, and how genome-wide testing can help assess risks, all while emphasizing that genetics is only one piece of the puzzle. What Are Speech Delays? A speech delay (or language delay) occurs when a young child is slower to develop communication skills than typical for their age. For example, a toddler might have a limited vocabulary or trouble forming sentences well past the expected milestone ages. Speech delays can range from mild (catching up with minimal intervention) to more significant delays requiring speech therapy. Often, speech delay is one aspect of a broader developmental delay or related to conditions like autism or developmental language disorder. Identifying a speech delay early allows for interventions to help the child progress. Genetic Factors in Speech and Language Development Research shows that genetics play a significant role in speech and language development. Developmental delays (including speech delays) often run in families, suggesting a heritable component. In fact, studies indicate that over 30% of diagnosed developmental delay cases are associated with an identifiable genetic cause (Is there genetic testing for Intellectual Disability and Developmental Delay?). Scientists have discovered specific genes that impact speech – a famous example is the FOXP2 gene. A rare mutation in FOXP2 can lead to a severe speech and language disorder, as seen in one multigenerational family where an altered FOXP2 gene caused difficulties in producing intelligible speech. However, most common speech delays are polygenic (involving many genes) and complex. Twin studies further support genetic influence, consistently finding higher similarity in speech abilities between identical twins than fraternal twins (Is Speech Delay Genetic? - Kutest Kids). These findings underscore that genetic factors contribute to speech delay risk, although no single gene is usually responsible in typical cases. Inherited vs. De Novo Genetic Mutations Genetic contributions to speech delays can be inherited or de novo. Inherited means a child receives gene variants from a parent that may predispose them to speech or language difficulties (for example, a parent with a history of late talking might pass on similar genetic factors). In contrast, de novo mutations are new genetic changes that arise in the embryo, not present in either parent. Many neurodevelopmental disorders that include speech delay occur due to de novo mutations. For instance, over 99% of cases of Rett syndrome – a condition that causes severe developmental regression including loss of speech – are caused by a random new mutation with no family history (Is there genetic testing for Intellectual Disability and Developmental Delay?). This means that even parents with no family history of speech or language issues can have a child with a genetically driven delay. Understanding this difference is important for families: an inherited risk might be suspected from family history, whereas de novo causes are largely unpredictable without advanced genetic screening. Genome-Wide Testing to Assess Risk Thanks to advances in genomics, whole-genome embryo testing (like Orchid’s PGT) now allows prospective parents to screen for numerous genetic variants associated with neurodevelopmental conditions before pregnancy. Orchid’s embryo genome screening reads the embryo’s entire DNA, focusing on genes and chromosome regions linked to developmental disorders. This includes hundreds of genetic changes – both inherited and de novo – known to cause intellectual disabilities, developmental delays, or other neurodevelopmental disorders. By doing such testing, parents can assess if an embryo carries specific genetic mutations that research has tied to speech or language-related conditions (for example, certain forms of autism or rare speech apraxia syndromes). Importantly, if a known high-risk variant is found, parents and doctors can make informed decisions – such as selecting a different embryo or planning early interventions. Genome-wide PGT provides a powerful risk assessment tool for speech-delay-related conditions that were previously “unknowable before delivery” (Genetic Testing for Autism, Intellectual Disability, and other Neurodevelopmental Disorders). However, it’s crucial to remember that no test can detect every possible cause of speech delays (Is there genetic testing for Intellectual Disability and Developmental Delay?). A negative result does not guarantee a child will have no issues, just as a positive result indicates risk rather than certainty. Genetics Is Only One Piece of the Puzzle While genetics are important, they are only one part of the puzzle. In many children, speech delays arise from a mix of genetic and environmental factors. fetched_contents.text: Developmental Surveillance and Screening Patient Care Welcome to American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) Developmental Surveillance and Screening Initiatives pages. Watch our brief video to learn more about the AAP's recommendations and guidance on developmental disabilites. Web pages whose development was supported by federal government grants are being reviewed to comply with applicable Executive Orders. Given the prevalence of developmental delays and disabilities, all pediatric primary care clinicians should be prepared to screen, identify, and care for children and youth with developmental delays and disabilities and their families. Activities to promote developmental surveillance and screening are implemented across numerous Academy initiatives, including Bright Futures, the Council on Children with Disabilities, Council on Early Childhood, Section on Developmental and Behavioral Pediatrics, and the Screening Technical Assistance and Resource (STAR) Center. Below you will find information about developmental surveillance and screening tools and resources for pediatricians. Resources for parents, families, and caregivers are available on the AAP parenting website, HealthyChildren.org. AAP Policies and Clinical Reports What is the Difference Between Developmental Surveillance and Developmental Screening? It is important to understand how developmental surveillance is different from developmental screening. Developmental Surveillance is an important way for clinicians to identify children at risk for developmental delay and should occur during every health supervision visit. During these visits, clinicians should address developmental progress, concerns, and promotion. AAP recommends conducting developmental surveillance at every health supervision visit, with special attention at the 4- to 5-year visit as the child prepares to enter elementary school. Developmental surveillance resources can be integrated into office procedures. Six components of developmental surveillance 1. Eliciting parent’s concerns 2. Obtaining a developmental history 3. Observing the child 4. Identifying risks, strengths, and protective factors 5. Maintaining a record 6. Sharing opinions and findings Developmental screening supplements and strengthens ongoing developmental surveillance to identify subtle risks for developmental delays that parents and pediatricians may not recognize during routine interactions. General developmental screening tests should be conducted at the 9-, 18-, and 30-month health supervision visit. Autism spectrum disorder screening tests should be conducted at the 18- and 24- month health supervision visits. Screening tests should also be administered when a clinician, parents, or early childhood professionals have concerns during surveillance or at any other time concerns arise. Screening involves the use of validated, standardized screening tests used universally at specific ages, as well as when developmental surveillance reveals a concern. It’s very important to remember that surveillance is NOT screening and should not be thought to take the place of a validated screening tool. Think of surveillance as working together with those specific screening tools! Pediatric practices can customize this guide with information about local referral resources, and then use the guide to support families/caregivers in understanding what to do if a developmental concern has been identified. The guide also illustrates the importance of following through with developmental referrals. English Spanish Learn the Signs. Act Early. Lipkin, MD, FAAP, lead author of the clinical report. “With continued surveillance, early learning and attention problems often become more apparent by age 4 or 5. ## Red flags and developmental history to gather from the mother

The mother should be asked to provide a detailed developmental history and observe specific milestones that are expected at 2 years of age. The CDC notes that developmental milestones are things most children do by 2 years and that how a child plays, learns, speaks, acts, and moves offers important clues about development [N2-F2]. A 2-year-old is expected to point to things in a book when asked, say at least two words together, point to at least two body parts when asked, and use more gestures than just waving and pointing [N2-F2]. The child should also be able to kick a ball, run, walk up a few stairs with or without help, and eat with a spoon [N2-F2]. These milestones help the physician assess whether the child is meeting expected developmental benchmarks.

Red flags indicating more urgent evaluation are also important. The CDC page emphasizes that the mother should share whether the child has lost any skills she once had or whether there are any special healthcare needs or a history of being born prematurely [N2-F2]. Other red flags in the evidence include not responding to loud noises, not watching things as they move, and not bringing hands to objects [N2-R4]. The CDC also notes that parents should be attentive if a child does not respond to their name consistently, does not play appropriately, or has unusual social or emotional behaviors [N2-F2]. In the context of a 2-year-old not talking, the mother should also be asked whether the child uses two-word phrases, follows basic directions, copies actions, or uses gestures beyond simple waving and pointing [N2-R3]. These signs can point to a more significant delay or underlying condition.

Family history and other background information are also critical. The evidence shows that genetics and family history can play a role in speech and language development, with developmental delays often running in families [N4-F3]. It also notes that family-based risk factors studied include multilingual family environment, high birth order, consanguinity, and family history of speech-language delay [N4-R1]. Other risk factors mentioned in the evidence include male gender, first-born birth order, and a family history of developmental delay [N4-R3]. Environmental factors include maternal educational level, number of siblings, and socio-economic status [N4-R4]. The mother should therefore be asked about her child’s family history of speech delay, any known developmental concerns in siblings or relatives, and any environmental or social factors that may have changed recently [N4-F3][N4-R1][N4-R4]. The physician may also need to know whether the child has been exposed to consistent verbal engagement, has had any ear infections or hearing concerns, or has had limited opportunities for interactive language learning [N4-F3].

In short, the mother’s history should be organized around: 1) which milestones the child has met or not met, 2) any skills that have regressed or been lost, 3) any red flags in social, communication, motor, or cognitive domains, and 4) family and environmental risk factors [N2-F2][N2-R4][N4-F3][N4-R1]. This information helps determine whether further workup is needed and guides the next steps in evaluation.

## How screening tools fit into the clinical workflow and what they tell the physician

In clinical practice, screening tools are used as part of a broader developmental workflow that combines surveillance with formal assessment. The AAP explains that developmental surveillance is conducted at every health supervision visit and is used to identify children at risk for developmental delay, while developmental screening supplements surveillance with validated, standardized tools at specific ages [N5-F1]. The CDC similarly says that the tools used for developmental screening are formal questionnaires or checklists based on research and that developmental screening should be conducted at the 9-, 18-, and 30-month visits, with autism screening at 18 and 24 months [N5-R4]. For a 2-year-old not talking, screening tools help the physician identify subtle risks that routine conversation may miss, especially when concerns are raised by the parent or by early childhood professionals [N5-F1].

The most commonly used screening tools in practice are the Parents’ Evaluation of Developmental Status and the Ages and Stages Questionnaire, as noted in the AAP evidence [N5-R3]. The AAP also mentions that the CDC’s Learn the Signs. Act Early program provides milestone checklists and a Milestone Tracker mobile app for parents to track development and share information with the pediatrician [N5-F1]. These tools are not meant to replace evaluation, but they are useful for gathering a structured developmental history and identifying patterns that may signal a delay [N5-F1]. The mother’s use of these tools can help the physician understand whether the child is meeting expected milestones in speech, motor, problem-solving, and social domains [N5-R1][N5-R3].

The results of screening tools influence the need for further workup. If a child is not meeting milestones or if screening raises concerns, the physician should ask for a referral to a specialist and consider more detailed evaluation [N2-F2][N5-F1]. The AAP specifically states that screening should be conducted when concerns arise during surveillance and that it is especially important to screen at 18 and 24 months for autism spectrum disorder [N5-F1]. In the context of a child not talking, a positive or concerning screening result would likely prompt a hearing assessment and a speech-language referral [N2-F2][N5-F1]. The evidence also shows that screening can identify subtle risks that parents and pediatricians may not recognize during routine interactions, so the physician may decide to pursue more specialized assessment even if screening alone is not diagnostic [N5-F1].

Screening tools have important limitations. The AAP emphasizes that surveillance is not screening and should not be thought to replace a validated screening tool [N5-F1]. The evidence also notes that developmental screening should be used when concerns arise during surveillance, but it does not provide a complete evaluation of the child’s development [N5-F1]. The USPSTF evidence on speech and language delay screening indicates that there was adequate evidence on the accuracy of screening tools to detect speech and language delay and disorders, but there were limitations in the evidence base [N6-R2]. The AAP also notes that developmental screening is only one part of the clinical workflow and that it should be combined with developmental surveillance [N5-F1]. Therefore, screening tools are helpful but not definitive; they signal the need for further evaluation rather than replacing it [N5-F1][N6-R2]. The mother should understand that screening gives a snapshot of development, but the physician will still need a formal assessment, especially when a child is not talking [N5-F1][N6-R2].

If the mother reports that her child is not responding to her voice, not imitating sounds or actions, or not engaging in interactive play, that is especially concerning [N2-F2][N2-R3]. These are important clues that the child may need a more detailed evaluation.

## 3. Family history and other relevant background information

The mother should be asked about family history because genetics and family history can play a role in speech and language development. The evidence shows that developmental delays often run in families, and that family history of speech-language delay is a relevant risk factor [N4-F3][N4-R1]. The mother should be asked whether there is a history of speech delay or developmental concerns in siblings or relatives, and whether there are any known family-based risk factors such as multilingual environment, high birth order, consanguinity, or a family history of speech-language delay [N4-R1][N4-F3].

The mother should also be asked about other environmental and social factors that may affect development. The evidence mentions that male gender, first-born birth order, and a family history of developmental delay are associated with increased risk [N4-R3]. It also notes that environmental factors such as maternal educational level, number of siblings, and socio-economic status can be relevant [N4-R4]. The mother should be asked whether there have been changes in the home environment, whether the child has had limited verbal engagement, or whether there have been any chronic ear infections or hearing concerns [N4-F3]. This information helps identify whether the delay may have a genetic, environmental, or medical component.

## 4. Possible missing workup steps

The mother should understand that the most commonly recommended workup for a 2-year-old not talking usually starts with a hearing assessment and a formal speech-language evaluation. The CDC notes that if a child is not meeting one or more milestones, has lost skills, or the parent has other concerns, the next step is to ask for a referral to a specialist and to contact the state’s early intervention program [N2-F2]. The AAP also emphasizes that developmental screening and surveillance are part of routine care, but they are not sufficient on their own when concerns arise [N5-F1].

The mother should expect that hearing assessment is a standard next step, because hearing loss can cause speech delay and is a treatable cause [N2-F2]. She should also expect that a speech-language referral is needed to evaluate communication skills directly [N2-F2][N5-F1]. The evidence also supports the use of standardized, validated tools at specific ages to identify developmental delays [N5-F1]. In practice, this means the physician may use a formal checklist or milestone tracker to organize the evaluation [N2-F2][N5-F1].

Additional evaluations may be required based on the child’s history. If the mother’s history suggests a more complex developmental profile, the physician may recommend further workup such as an autism evaluation, a hearing assessment, and a more comprehensive speech-language evaluation [N5-F1][N4-F3]. The evidence also suggests that the child may need broader developmental assessment if there are concerns about broader developmental delays or if there is a family history of speech delay or other developmental issues [N1-R3][N4-F3].

## 5. What to ask the physician or pediatrician next

The mother should ask the physician or pediatrician several specific questions. First, she should ask whether the child’s hearing has been assessed, because the evidence clearly treats hearing assessment as a standard next step when speech delay is present [N2-F2]. She should also ask whether a formal speech-language evaluation is needed and what the next steps would be after that [N1-R3][N5-F1]. She should ask whether there are any red flags that suggest a more urgent workup, such as hearing loss, loss of skills, or concerns about other developmental domains [N2-F2][N4-F3]. She should also ask whether the physician would recommend developmental screening or other tools, and whether the clinic has a family-friendly referral guide or local resources to help with referrals [N5-F1]. Finally, she should ask whether the child’s family and environmental history changes the plan for evaluation [N4-F3].

## 6. What to expect from hearing and speech-language services

The mother should expect that the hearing service will evaluate whether the child hears well, because hearing loss is a common and treatable cause of delayed speech [N2-F2]. The speech-language service will then assess the child’s speech and language skills using standardized tests and will look for milestones in speech [N1-R3]. The AAP emphasizes that screening uses validated, standardized tools at specific ages to identify developmental delays, and that developmental screening supplements surveillance [N5-F1]. So the mother can expect the hearing specialist to determine whether hearing is a contributing factor and the speech-language pathologist to evaluate vocabulary, sentence structure, comprehension, and social communication [N1-R3][N5-F1].

The mother should also expect that the physician may use a checklist or milestone tracker to help organize the evaluation [N2-F2][N5-F1]. If the child is referred for a formal evaluation, the mother can anticipate a more detailed assessment of communication skills, language development, and whether there are signs of broader developmental concerns [N2-F2][N1-R3].

## 7. What to do while waiting for further evaluation

While waiting for further evaluation, the mother should continue to observe and document the child’s development closely. The CDC says the mother should share with the doctor what the child likes to do, what the child does or does not do that concerns her, and whether the child has lost any skills [N2-F2]. The evidence also says that how the child plays, learns, speaks, acts, and moves provides important clues about development [N2-F2]. In practical terms, the mother should note whether the child responds to her voice, uses gestures or words, follows directions, imitates sounds or actions, and interacts socially with others [N2-F2][N4-F3].

The mother should keep track of any changes in behavior, such as lack of eye contact, difficulty understanding simple commands, or limited vocalizations [N2-F2][N4-F3]. The AAP recommends using developmental surveillance during every health supervision visit and suggests that the mother can use milestone checklists and apps to track progress [N5-F1]. So the mother can use these tools to provide more complete information when the physician asks for a history and should continue supporting language learning through consistent verbal interaction, reading, and play [N2-F2][N5-F1].

## 8. How screening tools fit into the clinical workflow

Screening tools are part of the broader developmental workflow that combines surveillance with formal assessment. The AAP explains that developmental surveillance is conducted at every health supervision visit and is used to identify children at risk for developmental delay, while developmental screening supplements surveillance with validated, standardized tools at specific ages [N5-F1]. The CDC similarly says that the tools used for developmental screening are formal questionnaires or checklists based on research and that developmental screening should be conducted at the 9-, 18-, and 30-month visits, with autism screening at 18 and 24 months [N5-R4]. For a 2-year-old not talking, screening tools help the physician identify subtle risks that routine conversation may miss, especially when concerns are raised by the parent or by early childhood professionals [N5-F1].

The most commonly used screening tools in practice are the Parents’ Evaluation of Developmental Status and the Ages and Stages Questionnaire, as noted in the AAP evidence [N5-R3]. The AAP also mentions that the CDC’s Learn the Signs. Act Early program provides milestone checklists and a Milestone Tracker mobile app for parents to track development and share information with the pediatrician [N5-F1]. These tools are not meant to replace evaluation, but they are useful for gathering a structured developmental history and identifying patterns that may signal a delay [N5-F1]. The mother’s use of these tools can help the physician understand whether the child is meeting expected milestones in speech, motor, problem-solving, and social domains [N5-R1][N5-R3].

## 9. Limitations of screening tools and why they are not a substitute for evaluation

The evidence shows that screening tools are helpful but not definitive. The AAP emphasizes that surveillance is not screening and should not be thought to replace a validated screening tool [N5-F1]. The evidence also notes that developmental screening should be used when concerns arise during surveillance, but it does not provide a complete evaluation of the child’s development [N5-F1]. The USPSTF evidence on speech and language delay screening indicates that there was adequate evidence on the accuracy of screening tools to detect speech and language delay and disorders, but there were limitations in the evidence base [N6-R2]. The AAP also notes that developmental screening is only one part of the clinical workflow and that it should be combined with developmental surveillance [N5-F1]. Therefore, screening tools are helpful but not a substitute for a formal evaluation, especially when a child is not talking [N5-F1][N6-R2].

## 10. Practical conclusion for the mother

In summary, the mother should expect that the next steps likely include a hearing assessment and a speech-language referral, especially if the child is not talking and the history suggests concern [N2-F2][N1-R3]. She should also expect that the physician may use screening tools such as milestone checklists or standardized questionnaires to help identify whether further workup is needed [N5-F1][N5-R1]. While waiting for evaluation, the mother should continue to observe and document the child’s development, noting milestones, any red flags, and any changes in behavior [N2-F2][N4-F3]. She should also ask the physician about hearing, speech-language referral, and any additional evaluations that may be needed based on the child’s history [N2-F2][N4-F3][N5-F1]. Overall, the mother’s detailed history and the use of screening tools are important pieces of the evaluation, but they are not a substitute for a formal assessment [N5-F1][N6-R2].
